t: The Canaanites honoured a pantheon headed by El and his consort Asherah, with Baal Hadad, the storm god who brought the rain, and Anat, Astarte, Dagon and Resheph among the other deities.
Most of what is known comes from the clay tablets of Ugarit, dated around 1275 BCE, which preserve the Baal Cycle and other myths with hymns, prayers and ritual texts.

In the first millennium BCE its branches lived on among Phoenicians, Arameans and Moabites, many scholars count Israelite Yahwism among them, and Phoenician settlers carried it west as the Punic religion.
dyk: In the Baal Cycle the storm god Baal is swallowed by Mot, Death, and a terrible drought follows, until the goddess Anat attacks Mot with a knife, grinds him to pieces and scatters him, so that Baal can return and refresh the earth with rain.
ev: The Ebla tablets from Tell Mardikh in Syria list offerings to El, Baal and Dagon, the earliest evidence of Canaanite religion
Inscriptions of Idrimi, king of Alalakh, shed further light on Canaanite religion
The Ugaritic texts, more than three hundred of them on Canaanite myths, rites and prayers, date from about this time
Phoenicians found Carthage and other Punic communities in the western Mediterranean
The Mesha Stele is set up in Moab, one of the few sources for religion in the southern Levant beyond Israel and Judah
The Roman Republic conquers the Punic lands, where Punic religious practice continues
The last Punic religious practices die out

f.origin: the land of Canaan in the southern Levant, during approximately the first three millennia BCE; first attested in the Ebla tablets of the second half of the 3rd millennium BCE
f.founder: none: a tradition of many peoples and cities, strongly influenced by its Egyptian and Mesopotamian neighbours
f.scriptures: no scripture: myths, hymns, prayers and ritual texts on clay tablets, above all the Ugaritic texts of about 1275 BCE, with later inscriptions, the accounts of the Hebrew Bible and Greek writers such as Philo of Byblos
f.followers: none: its last branch, the Punic religion of the western Mediterranean, survived in some places until the 4th century CE
